interactions.summary: The host asks Jiang to compare the Canadian and Chinese education systems from experience.
Jiang contrasts Canada's equity-oriented uniformity with China's elitist sorting machine, arguing that the Chinese system judges children far too early.
The host asks how the Gaokao shapes pressure on students, parents, and teachers.
Jiang explains the Gaokao as a fair-seeming allocator of scarce opportunities that also creates a childhood-crushing pressure regime from the earliest years.
The host asks why Chinese families keep sending children abroad if the domestic system supposedly performs so well.
Jiang calls this the paradox of China's school system: public prestige after PISA coexists with affluent families fleeing a system they believe is harming their only child.

claims.claim: Jiang says Canadian education is organized around equity and mobility, with relatively even schools and an emphasis on making the most of the student's experience.
He describes China as a competitive elitist system that sorts students from day one through feeder schools into top universities.
Jiang argues early test scores are a poor basis for deciding a child's eventual adult performance, making the Chinese sorting system unfair.
He says the Gaokao is viewed in China as the fairest objective way to allocate scarce educational resources, even as it produces rigorous testing and parental pressure from early childhood.

Jiang says affluent Chinese families increasingly choose Canada, New Zealand, and the United States because they believe the domestic school system is hurting their child's curiosity, creativity, and imagination.

signature_moments.moment: China is described not as a neutral meritocracy but as a pipeline that sorts children from their first school day.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It captures Jiang's core critique that Chinese education is structurally hierarchical from the start, not just exam-heavy at the end.

signature_moments.moment: The Gaokao does not just add stress; it kills childhood itself.
signature_moments.source_phrase: a death of childhood in China
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is the packet's sharpest moral compression of Jiang's case against test-centered schooling.

signature_moments.moment: China's global PISA prestige is set against an internal exodus by the very parents who can afford to leave.
signature_moments.source_phrase: that's really the paradox of China's school system right now
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It preserves the contradiction between public admiration and private flight that drives the interview.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: China's national college entrance examination, treated here as the main mechanism for distributing scarce higher-education opportunity.

chronology_notes.note: By 2014 Jiang describes both a fully entrenched Gaokao pressure system and a recent countertrend of wealthy families emigrating or sending children abroad to escape it.

uncertainty_notes.note: The long repetition of the age-six versus age-18 line appears to be ASR duplication rather than deliberate rhetorical repetition, but the substantive point about non-linear development is clear.
